items.query_text: What is reconciliation in React and what are its high level phases?
items.goldAnswer: Reconciliation in React is the process React uses to determine what changes to make in the real DOM by comparing the new Virtual DOM with the previous Virtual DOM snapshot. High-level phases include Render Phase (JSX to new Virtual DOM), Diffing Phase (compare old and new VDOM trees to find differences), and Commit Phase (apply minimal changes to real DOM).

Page: 24th January

## What is rendering ?

Rendering is the process where React runs your component function (or render method) to determine what the UI should look like for the current state and props, producing a Virtual DOM tree.

FYI:

> Rendering does not mean updating the browser DOM — it only means computing the UI description.

```javascript
State / Props change
        ↓
Render phase
(component function runs)
        ↓
New Virtual DOM created
        ↓
Diff with old Virtual DOM
        ↓
Changes found?
   ├─ No → stop
   └─ Yes → commit phase
                 ↓
           Update real DOM
```

- Rendering does not update the real DOM

- Rendering only produces a UI description (Virtual DOM)

- That description is later used to decide DOM updates

## What is a virtual DOM ?

Common definition:

“Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the real DOM”

My definition:

A pure JavaScript object tree that describes what the UI should look like, independent of the browser.

### What Virtual DOM is NOT

Virtual DOM is not:

- A copy of the real DOM

- A browser structure

- Something with layout or styles computed

- Something the browser understands

The browser never sees Virtual DOM.

Hello

``` Virtual DOM (conceptually): ```javascript { type:"h1", props: { className:"title", children:"Hello" } } ``` This is just data. No width. No height. No pixels. No layout. ### Why “representation of real DOM” is misleading Because: - Virtual DOM can exist without any real DOM - Server rendering - React Native - Virtual DOM may describe UI that never gets rendered - It’s possible to render Virtual DOM multiple times without touching real DOM So it’s better to say: > Virtual DOM represents intended UI, not actual DOM. ### Correct mental model ```javascript State ↓ Render ↓ Virtual DOM (UI description) ↓ Diff (reconciliation) ↓ Real DOM mutations (if needed) ``` ## What is Reconciliation? items.query_text: Which algorithm is used for React tree comparison and what are its key assumptions?
items.goldAnswer: React uses a heuristic O(n) diffing algorithm instead of an O(n^3) tree diff. It relies on two main assumptions: 1) Two elements of different types will produce different trees (React unmounts the old subtree and mounts the new one), and 2) The developer can hint which child elements may be stable across different renders with a key prop.

Page: 24th January
Topic: What is diffing algorithm > Visual flow

```plain text
Old VDOM           New VDOM
---------          ---------
<div>      !==     <span>
  ├─ h1                └─ "Hello"
  └─ p
```

#### Assumption 2

> Children of the same type can be compared positionally (unless keys exist)

This is where keys come in.

---

### High-level diffing steps

For each node:

1. Compare type

1. Compare key

1. If same → update props

1. If different → replace subtree

This is O(1) per node.

---

### List diffing (where complexity matters)

#### Without keys

```javascript
[A, B, C]
[B, A, C]
```

React compares by index:

```plain text
A vs B → replace
B vs A → replace
C vs C → reuse
```

This is fast but inefficient in behavior.

---

#### With keys

```javascript
[A(id=1),B(id=2),C(id=3)]
[B(id=2),A(id=1),C(id=3)]
```

React:

1. Builds a key → index map

1. Matches nodes by key

1. Reorders efficiently

---

### Time complexity

#### Generic tree diff (theoretical)

- O(n³) (too slow)

- Impossible for real-time UI

---

Page: 24th January
Topic: What is diffing algorithm > Time complexity > React diffing complexity

- O(n) in most cases

- O(n) for keyed lists

- O(n) for tree traversal

This is why React scales.

---

### Why React diffing is fast in practice

Because React:

- Does NOT compare subtrees deeply

- Uses identity (type + key)

- Stops early when types differ

- Skips work aggressively

---

### Is diffing always efficient?

“No”.

#### Diffing becomes inefficient when:

- Keys are wrong (index keys)

- Large lists reorder frequently

- Components re-render unnecessarily

- Inline objects/functions cause re-renders

---

### 8️⃣ Example of inefficient diffing

```javascript
items.map((item, index) => (
    <Item key={index} {...item} />
))
```

Reordering list → React destroys and recreates components.

Diffing still runs in O(n), but DOM churn increases.

## Comparison of react architecture :

## What is Stack Reconciler

“Stack Reconciler was React’s old rendering engine that used a synchronous diffing algorithm and the JavaScript call stack to perform reconciliation and DOM updates.”

- Algorithm = the logic for comparing trees

- Rendering engine = the system that:

- runs the algorithm

- walks the component tree

- schedules work

- applies DOM updates

Stack Reconciler was the original algorithm React used to:

> Compare old Virtual DOM with new Virtual DOM

and update the real DOM

---

items.query_text: What are closures in JavaScript and what is a practical example of where they are used?
items.goldAnswer: A closure is a function combined with its lexical environment. When an inner function is defined inside an outer function, it retains access to variables declared in the outer function even after the outer function has returned. Practical examples include data privacy/encapsulation (private variables), function factories, and memoization/currying.

items.query_text: How is JavaScript code executed, including execution context creation and execution phases?
items.goldAnswer: JavaScript code runs inside execution contexts managed by a Call Stack. Each execution context is created in two phases: 1) Creation/Memory Allocation Phase: variables are allocated memory with undefined (or uninitialized for let/const) and function declarations are stored in memory; 2) Code Execution Phase: code executes line-by-line assigning real values and invoking functions.

Page: 10th January - JavaScript Basics
Topic: Topic 2: Execution context > What is it physically?

#### Physically, an execution context is:

- A C++ object / struct

- Allocated in native memory (heap)

- Created and destroyed by the JS engine (e.g., V8)

- Referenced by the call stack

You can think of it as:

```javascript
// Conceptual (NOT real V8 code)
struct ExecutionContext {
LexicalEnvironment* lexicalEnv;
VariableEnvironment* variableEnv;
ThisBinding thisValue;
CodePointer* instructionPointer;
};
```

📌 This is not the real implementation, but it is conceptually accurate.

### Where does it live?

#### In memory, not in JavaScript land

- Execution contexts live in engine-managed memory

- Not accessible from JavaScript

- Not visible in DevTools

- Exist only while code is executing

The Call Stack is essentially:

> A stack of pointers to these execution context objects.

---

### How the call stack fits physically

Visualize this:

```plain text
Call Stack (native memory)
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Pointer → EC forfoo()   │
│ Pointer → EC forbar()   │
│ Pointer → Global EC     │
└─────────────────────────┘
```

Each stack frame points to:

- One execution context object

- Which contains references to scopes, variables, and instructions

items.query_text: What is the difference between Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation and Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) compilation?
items.goldAnswer: In AOT compilation, code is compiled into machine code or optimized bytecode before runtime (during build time). In JIT compilation (used by modern engines like V8), code starts as interpreted bytecode and hot functions are monitored by a profiler and compiled into optimized machine code during runtime execution.

Page: 10th January - JavaScript Basics
Topic: Topic 2: Execution context

### What is an Execution Context?

> Execution Context is the environment in which JavaScript code is evaluated and executed.

Every time JavaScript runs code, it does so inside an execution context.

At any moment:

- Only one execution context is active

- It always sits on top of the Call Stack

---

### Types of Execution Context

JavaScript has two main execution contexts:

1. Global Execution Context (GEC)

1. Function Execution Context (FEC)

---

### Global Execution Context (GEC)

#### What is Global Execution Context?

- Created once when the JavaScript file starts executing. (Files are just sources of code, not runtime boundaries.)

- Represents code not inside any function

- Sits at the bottom of the call stack

---

#### What does GEC contain?

The Global Execution Context has two phases:

#### 1️⃣ Memory Creation Phase (Creation Phase)

Before executing a single line of code, JavaScript:

- Allocates memory

- Sets up scope

During this phase:

- var variables → initialized as undefined

- Function declarations → fully hoisted

- let & const → allocated but not initialized

- this → points to the global object (browser: window)

---

items.query_text: What are higher-order components (HOC) in React and why are they used over simple utilities?

Unlike utility functions that only perform computations or network calls, an HOC injects UI props, manages lifecycle states, or wraps UI layouts around target components without altering the original component code.

items.query_text: If a three-second delay is given to setTimeout, will it definitely execute after 3 seconds, and why?
items.goldAnswer: No, the 3-second delay is not guaranteed to be exact. It represents a minimum delay. Once the timer completes in Web APIs, the callback is pushed into the macrotask queue. It can only execute once the call stack is completely empty and any pending microtasks have finished running.

Page: 10th January - JavaScript Basics
Topic: Topic 1: What is JavaScript Runtime? > Task Queues > Macrotask Queue

- Lower priority queue

- Contains:

- setTimeout

- setInterval

- DOM events

Microtasks are always executed before macrotasks.

---

### Event Loop

The event loop continuously checks the call stack and queues.

Execution order:

1. Call stack must be empty

1. Execute all microtasks

1. Execute one macrotask

1. Repeat the cycle

The event loop coordinates execution between the call stack and queues.

---

### Complete Execution Example

```javascript
console.log("A");

setTimeout(() => {
   console.log("B");
},0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
   console.log("C");
});

console.log("D");
```

Execution order:

- A is logged

- setTimeout callback is registered with Web API

- Promise callback is added to microtask queue

- D is logged

- Call stack becomes empty

- Microtask queue executes → C

- Macrotask queue executes → B

Final Output:

```plain text
A
D
C
B
```

---

Page: 10th January - JavaScript Basics
Topic: Topic 1: What is JavaScript Runtime? > Key Takeaways

- JavaScript executes code using a single call stack

- Asynchronous operations are handled by browser Web APIs

- Microtasks have higher priority than macrotasks

- Event loop decides execution order

- setTimeout(0) does not mean immediate execution

---

### How is Event Loop different from JS Engine (V8) ?

“The event loop is a browser-side scheduler that coordinates when the JavaScript engine can execute queued callbacks.”

### Why doesn’t the JS Engine include the Event Loop?

Because JavaScript is designed to be host-agnostic.

The same JS engine can run in:

- Browser

- Node.js

- Deno

- Embedded systems

Each environment provides:

- Its own APIs

- Its own event loop implementation

Example:

- Browser Event Loop ≠ Node.js Event Loop

- V8 is reused, but event loop is replaced

### Summary

JavaScript is single-threaded and synchronous by default.

The browser runtime enables asynchronous behavior using Web APIs, task queues, and the event loop.

items.query_text: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) and how does hoisting work for let and const?
items.goldAnswer: The Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) is the period between entering a scope and the actual line of code where a let or const variable is declared and initialized. While let and const are hoisted to the top of their block scope, they remain uninitialized in the TDZ; accessing them before initialization throws a ReferenceError.

```javascript

   console.log("Hi");
}
```

What happens:

- Entire function is hoisted

- Function can be called before declaration

📌 Key point:

> Function declarations are fully hoisted

#### let and const Hoisting

```javascript
console.log(b);
let b = 20
```

Result:

```plain text
ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
```

What happens:

- b is hoisted

- But not initialized

- Exists in Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)

📌 Key point:

> let and const are hoisted but not usable before initialization

---

#### Function Expressions

```javascript
sayHello();

var sayHello = function () {
   console.log("Hello");
};
```

What happens:

- sayHello is hoisted as undefined

- Function body is not hoisted

Result:

```plain text
TypeError: sayHello is not a function
```

📌 Key point

> Function expressions follow variable hoisting rules

---

items.query_text: Why did React need the Fiber architecture and what are the phases in Fiber?
items.goldAnswer: React needed Fiber to overcome the limitations of the synchronous Stack Reconciler, which blocked the main thread on deep component trees causing frame drops. Fiber introduces an incremental, cooperative scheduling engine with two phases: 1) Render Phase (asynchronous, interruptible diffing and fiber tree creation) and 2) Commit Phase (synchronous DOM mutations).

relevantChunks.text:
Page: 24th January
Topic: Why React Needed Fiber Architecture > Render Phases in Fiber

React Fiber has two main phases:

#### 1. Render Phase (Interruptible)

- Builds Fiber tree

- Computes changes

- Can pause / restart / discard

#### 2. Commit Phase (Non-interruptible)

- Applies DOM updates

- Runs effects

- Updates refs

---

#### Important Interview Line

> Render phase is interruptible, commit phase is not.

---

### How Fiber Helps Reconciliation

Without Fiber:

- React compared full trees in one go

With Fiber:

- React can compare small subtrees

- Pause between them

- Prioritize visible updates

This is what makes concurrent rendering possible.

---

### Concurrent Features Enabled by Fiber

Because of Fiber, React supports:

- startTransition

- useDeferredValue

- Concurrent rendering

- Streaming SSR

- Suspense

All of these depend on Fiber.

## Diffing in Fibre v/s Stack reconciler

### Stack reconciler

> Stack Reconciler itself contained and executed the diffing (reconciliation) algorithm.

More precisely:

- Stack Reconciler was the rendering engine

- Inside it lived

- the tree traversal logic

- the diffing logic (old VDOM vs new VDOM)

- the DOM mutation logic

- All of this ran synchronously on the JS call stack

There was no separate scheduler or layered system.

So the correct mental model is:

```plain text
StackReconciler
 ├─render traversal
 ├─diffing algorithm
 └─DOM updates
```

---

Page: 24th January
Topic: Why React Needed Fiber Architecture

Old React (before Fiber):

- Rendering was synchronous

- Once rendering started → it could not stop

- Big UI updates blocked browser

- Animations felt janky

React needed:

- Interruptible rendering

- Priority based updates

- Ability to pause and resume work

---

### What is Fiber?

Fiber is React’s new internal architecture.

It is:

> A data structure + scheduling system

that breaks rendering into small units of work.

---

#### Fiber enables:

- Time slicing

- Interruptible rendering

- Concurrent rendering

- Better scheduling

- Priority updates

---

#### Old Stack Reconciler

```plain text
Render starts → must finish fully → DOM updates
```

---

#### Fiber Reconciler

```plain text
Render starts
→ pause
→ handle high priority update
→ resume render
```

---

#### Mental Model

React no longer renders in one big task.

It renders in small fiber nodes.

Each component = one Fiber node.

---

#### Fiber Node Contains

- type

- props

- state

- child

- sibling

- parent

- effect flags (what side-effects need to be executed on that node during the Commit Phase)

This allows React to walk the tree in any order.

---

); } function Header() { return

Hello

; } function Content() { const [count, setCount] = React.useState(0); return

{count}

; } ``` #### Conceptual Fiber Tree (one Fiber per element/component) ```javascript [App Fiber] | v [div Fiber] | +--> [Header Fiber] ----> [h1 Fiber] | +--> [Content Fiber] ---> [p Fiber] ``` This is not the DOM. This is React’s Fiber tree in memory. #### Zoom into ONE Fiber Node (Content) ```javascript [Content Fiber] ──────────────────────────── type: Content props: {} state: { count: 0 } parent: div Fiber child: p Fiber sibling: null effectFlags: Update ``` #### How fibers connect Parent → Child → Sibling relationships ```javascript [div Fiber] / \ v v [Header Fiber] [Content Fiber] | | v v [h1 Fiber] [p Fiber] ```

Page: 24th January
Topic: React 19 — Architectural Direction > 3. Asset Loading Architecture

Scripts, styles, fonts are now scheduled via React itself.

React controls:

- When resources load

- In what priority

Using Fiber scheduler.

---

#### 4. Document Metadata Handling

```javascript
<title>
	<meta>
<link>
```

Now managed by React tree instead of manual head manipulation.

---

#### 5. Reduced useEffect Dependency

React 19 encourages:

- Fewer effects

- More direct data flow

- Better scheduling

---

### 9. Architectural Evolution Summary

## Why Keys Matter

#### Purpose of Keys

Keys help React identify which elements in a list have changed, been added, or removed so that reconciliation can work efficiently.

---

#### Keys — Good vs Bad (Real Architectural Impact)

Keys are not for React warnings.

Keys are for reconciliation identity.

React uses keys to decide:

> Is this the same component instance or a new one?

---

#### ❌ Bad Key Example

```javascript
{users.map((user, index) => (
		<UserCard key={index} user={user} />
))}
```
